```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(knitr)

# Synthetic teaching data for BIOS 6301. Not real patients.
set.seed(6301)
n <- 60
trial <- data.frame(
  id        = sprintf("P%03d", 1:n),
  arm       = rep(c("Placebo", "Treatment"), each = n / 2),
  site      = sample(1:4, n, replace = TRUE),
  age       = round(rnorm(n, 61, 9)),
  sex       = sample(c("F", "M"), n, replace = TRUE),
  weight_kg = round(rnorm(n, 82, 15), 1),
  sbp_0     = round(rnorm(n, 148, 14)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
trial$sbp_12 <- round(trial$sbp_0 -
  ifelse(trial$arm == "Treatment", rnorm(n, 14, 8), rnorm(n, 3, 8)))

# Added for this session: the derived outcome the refactoring demo summarises.
trial$change <- trial$sbp_12 - trial$sbp_0

# A copy carrying the two defects a real extract arrives with, used for the
# validation demos. What is broken, deliberately:
#   sbp_12    three missing 12-week outcomes (P007, P023, P048)
#   weight_kg one weight recorded as the sentinel -99 (P012)
trial_raw <- trial
trial_raw$sbp_12[c(7, 23, 48)] <- NA
trial_raw$weight_kg[12] <- -99
trial_raw$change <- trial_raw$sbp_12 - trial_raw$sbp_0

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 15))
```

# 1 · Conditions {.section-divider}

## A calculation can run and still be wrong {.smaller #a-report-needs-a-decision}

A script receives four baseline readings but only two follow-up readings.
It should flag the mismatch before calculating paired changes.

```{r}
#| label: condition-motivation
baseline <- c(150, 140, 160, 155)
followup <- c(138, 132)
followup - baseline
```

| Situation | What the script should do |
|---|---|
| Different numbers of readings | Flag the mismatch and skip the calculation |
| Equal numbers of already matched readings | Calculate follow-up minus baseline |

R reused the two follow-up values and returned **four changes without a warning**.
We need one decision about whether the calculation should run at all.


## What `if` does {.smaller}

`if` chooses which block of code runs. Its condition must give **one nonmissing
logical value**: `TRUE` or `FALSE`.

```r
if (condition) {
  # Run this block when the condition is TRUE.
} else {
  # Run this block when the condition is FALSE.
}
```

Use it when the next action depends on the current inputs: calculate paired
changes or report an input problem. Only the chosen branch runs.

## Check the inputs before calculating {.smaller #use-if-for-the-report-decision}

```{r}
#| label: if-report
if (length(followup) != length(baseline)) {
  "Check the input: baseline and follow-up counts differ"
} else {
  followup - baseline
}
```

The comparison of lengths gives **one `TRUE` or `FALSE`**. Here it is `TRUE`,
so R returns the message and does not run the subtraction in `else`.

Equal lengths are necessary; the readings must also belong to the same people
in the same order. This check cannot establish that alignment.

## More than two cases: `else if` {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: if-basic
n_missing <- sum(is.na(trial_raw$sbp_12))
if (n_missing == 0) {
  "No outcomes are missing"
} else if (n_missing == 1) {
  "One outcome is missing"
} else {
  "Multiple outcomes are missing"
}
```

Conditions are checked in order; the first matching branch runs. The final `else`
handles the remaining case. Keep `} else {` together and use braces for each block.

## A vector is not one decision {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: if-error
#| error: true
if (trial$sbp_0 > 140) "above cutoff" else "at or below cutoff"
```

```{r}
#| label: condition-length
head(trial$sbp_0 > 140)
length(trial$sbp_0 > 140)
```

There is one comparison per participant, but `if` requires one decision.
The repair depends on the intended question: **one label per participant**, or
**one answer about the whole group**? The cutoff is only a coding example.

## One label per participant: `ifelse()` {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: ifelse-repair
above <- trial$sbp_0 > 140
labels <- ifelse(above, "above cutoff", "at or below cutoff")
head(data.frame(sbp = trial$sbp_0, above, label = labels))
length(labels)
```

`ifelse()` makes an elementwise choice: one comparison and one returned label
per participant. This is the vectorized conditional introduced in Session 3.

It repairs the preceding code **if the goal is a label for every row**.

## One group decision: `any()` or `all()` {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: reduce-conditions
c(at_least_one = any(above), every_participant = all(above))

if (any(above)) {
  "At least one participant is above the cutoff"
} else {
  "No participant is above the cutoff"
}

if (all(above)) "Everyone is above" else "Not everyone is above"
```

`any()` and `all()` reduce the vector to one logical value, suitable for `if`.
They answer different group questions; neither produces a label for every row.
The measurements in this example are complete.

## Match the tool to the question {.smaller}

| Intended result | Tool |
|---|---|
| One action based on a single condition | `if (...) ... else ...` |
| One label for each value | `ifelse(test, yes, no)` |
| One action if at least one value meets a rule | `if (any(test)) ...` |
| One action if every value meets a rule | `if (all(test)) ...` |

An `if` expression can also supply a value for assignment:

```{r}
#| label: if-value
label <- if (n_missing > 0) "missing outcomes present" else "no missing outcomes"
label
```

## A missing condition is a separate problem {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: if-error-2
#| error: true
sbp <- NA_real_
if (sbp > 140) "above cutoff" else "at or below cutoff"
```

The condition has length one, but its value is unknown. Handle that case explicitly:

```{r}
#| label: if-missing-repair
if (is.na(sbp)) {
  "measurement missing"
} else if (sbp > 140) {
  "above cutoff"
} else {
  "at or below cutoff"
}
```

`NA` is not `FALSE`; missing measurements need a stated reporting rule.

## Missing values in a group decision {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: observed-group-decision
x <- c(120, NA, 155)
c(observed = sum(!is.na(x)),
  any_observed_above = any(x > 140, na.rm = TRUE),
  all_observed_above = all(x > 140, na.rm = TRUE))
```

`na.rm = TRUE` changes the question to the **observed** measurements. It does not
show what the missing measurements would have been.

Without removal, a missing comparison can leave `any()` or `all()` unresolved.
Report the observed count alongside a result that excludes missing values.

## An empty condition is a separate problem {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: if-error-3
#| error: true
sbp <- numeric(0)  # No values remain after filtering; this is not the number 0.
if (sbp > 140) "above cutoff"
```

Check availability before asking a question that requires observed data:

```{r}
#| label: if-empty-repair
if (sum(!is.na(sbp)) == 0) {
  "No observed measurements"
} else if (any(sbp > 140, na.rm = TRUE)) {
  "At least one observed measurement is above the cutoff"
} else {
  "No observed measurement is above the cutoff"
}
```

`all(logical(0))` is `TRUE` and `any(logical(0))` is `FALSE`.
Neither establishes that measurements were available.

## Scalar and elementwise operators {.smaller}

| Need | Operators | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Combine checks for each value | `&`, <code>&#124;</code> | `!is.na(x) & x > 140` |
| Combine single decisions | `&&`, <code>&#124;&#124;</code> | `length(x) > 0 && all(is.finite(x))` |

```{r}
#| label: short-circuit
candidate <- NA_real_
is.numeric(candidate) && length(candidate) == 1 &&
  !is.na(candidate) && candidate > 0
```

`&&` stops when the left check is false. Put shape and missingness checks
before a comparison that assumes one observed value.

## Practice 1: choose and repair {.smaller}

For each task, choose a vectorized conditional or one `if` decision.

1. Label every change as `"decrease"`, `"no decrease"`, or `"missing"`.
2. Stop if a required column is absent.
3. Report whether **any observed** change is negative.

Repair this code for task 3:

```r
change <- c(-2, NA, 1, 0)
if (change < 0) "a decrease was observed"
```

## Practice 1: discussion {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: condition-answer
change <- c(-2, NA, 1, 0)
ifelse(is.na(change), "missing",
       ifelse(change < 0, "decrease", "no decrease"))

if (any(change < 0, na.rm = TRUE)) {
  "a decrease was observed"
} else {
  "no observed decrease"
}
```

Tasks 2 and 3 each need one decision. Task 1 needs one label per value.
An all-missing input supports **no observed decrease**, not **no decrease**.

# 2 · Why functions? {.section-divider}


## Look at what you have been doing {.smaller}

```r
# session 6 — baseline SBP by arm
trial |> group_by(arm) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(sbp_0), sd = sd(sbp_0))

# session 7 — the same, after the join
trial |> group_by(arm) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(sbp_12), sd = sd(sbp_12))

# session 8 — weight, to annotate the figure
trial |> group_by(arm) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(weight_kg), sd = sd(weight_kg))

# coursework — age, for the baseline table
trial |> group_by(arm) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(age), sd = sd(age))
```

. . .

Four blocks. **One name differs.**


## What copy-paste actually costs {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size:0.88em"}
| Cost | What repeated copies make harder |
|---|---|
| **Reading** | A reader has to diff four blocks to find the one word that differs |
| **Changing** | If missing values arrive, update the missing-value policy in every copy; overlooking one gives inconsistent summaries |
| **Naming** | The block has no name, so you cannot say what it does, reuse it, or check it |
| **Divergence** | If one copy later adds `round(..., digits = 2)` and the others do not, the reporting rules diverge |
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
The preceding code does not round any results. Rounding is an example of a
future change that must be kept consistent across copies.
:::

. . .

By the end of today that block is one line:

```r
summarise_by_arm(trial, sbp_0)
```


## A contract before code {.smaller}

For a reusable summary, decide what the caller can rely on.

| Part | Decision |
|---|---|
| Input | A numeric vector, possibly containing missing values |
| Options | Rounding precision and whether to remove missing values |
| Output | Named values with a documented meaning for `n` |
| Edge cases | What happens with no observations or the wrong input type? |

**Quick discussion:** should `n` count all rows or observed measurements?
What label would make that choice clear?

# 3 · Function basics {.section-divider}

## Read the parts of a function call {.smaller}

Before writing a function, read the interface of one you already use.

```{r}
#| label: function-interface
median_result <- stats::median(x = c(120, NA, 140), na.rm = TRUE)
median_result
```

| Part | Meaning in this call |
|---|---|
| `stats::` | Select the function from the **stats package namespace** |
| `median` | Function name |
| `x = c(120, NA, 140)` | Supply the data argument |
| `na.rm = TRUE` | Supply an option controlling missing values |
| Returned value: `130` | The result, saved in `median_result` by `<-` |


## Package namespaces identify which function {.smaller}

A **namespace** holds a package's objects and keeps its names separate from
those in other packages. `package::function` selects an exported function.

| Explicit name | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `stats::median()` | Compute a median |
| `dplyr::filter()` | Select rows of a data frame |
| `stats::filter()` | Filter a time series, for example with a moving average |

- The package must be installed. `::` loads its namespace as needed.
- You do **not** need to call `library()` first.
- An explicit package name avoids confusion when packages share a function name.


## Parameters define the interface; arguments fill it {.smaller}

**Parameters**, or formal arguments, are the names in the definition.
The help page's **Usage** section shows them and their defaults:

```r
median(x, na.rm = FALSE, ...)
```

| Parameter | Meaning | Argument in our call |
|---|---|---|
| `x` | Data to summarize; no default | `c(120, NA, 140)` |
| `na.rm` | Remove missing values? Default: `FALSE` | `TRUE` |
| `...` | Further arguments for methods; unused by the default method | None supplied |

The **Arguments** section explains accepted inputs. Omitting `na.rm` uses
`FALSE`; supplying `na.rm = TRUE` overrides that default.


## The return value is an object you can use {.smaller}

Our call returned one numeric value, `130`. We saved it in `median_result`.
The help page's **Value** section describes the result's type and length.

```{r}
#| label: function-interface-value
typeof(median_result)
length(median_result)
median_result + 10
```

**Returning** makes an object available to the caller. **Printing** displays it.
Assignment stores the result without automatically printing it.


## Read the help page as a function contract {.smaller}

```r
help("median", package = "stats")
# Alternatively: ?stats::median
```

| Help section | Question it answers |
|---|---|
| **Description** | What does this function do? |
| **Usage** | How do I call it? Which defaults apply? |
| **Arguments** | What does each input mean and accept? |
| **Value** | What object comes back? What happens in edge cases? |
| **Details** | Which additional rules or methods matter? |
| **Examples / See Also** | How is it used? Which related functions may help? |

Section names vary: some pages describe the return value under **Details**.


## Check the contract before running the code {.smaller}

Use **Usage**, **Arguments**, and **Value** in `?stats::median` to predict:

- Which call removes the missing value?
- Does an empty input return an empty vector or one missing value?

. . .

```{r}
#| label: function-help-check
stats::median(c(120, NA, 140))
stats::median(c(120, NA, 140), na.rm = TRUE)
stats::median(numeric(0), na.rm = TRUE)
```

The results are `NA`, `130`, and `NA`, each of length one.
Now give your own function an equally clear input/output contract.


## Start with a calculation you can check {.smaller}

For three measurements, work out the answer before writing a function:
`n = 3`, mean `130`, and sample SD `10`.

```{r}
#| label: summary-reference
example_sbp <- c(120, 130, 140)
summary_reference <- c(n = length(example_sbp),
                       mean = mean(example_sbp), sd = sd(example_sbp))
summary_reference
```

The calculation is already useful. The next step is to make it work for a
different numeric vector without editing its body.


## Decide which parts belong in the interface {.smaller}

| Choice | Our decision | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Which measurements? | Required parameter `x` | The caller must choose the data |
| How much rounding? | Optional `digits = 1` | A common display choice, with an override |
| What comes back? | Named numeric vector: `n`, `mean`, `sd` | All three results are numeric |
| Which inputs initially? | Complete numeric vectors with at least two values | Establish a simple working version first |

Replace **every** use of `example_sbp` in the calculation with `x`.
Do not give `x` a default that silently selects a dataset from your workspace.


## Your first function, from your own code {.smaller}

First extract the numeric summary used inside each repeated block. Grouping
will return in Section 6; this helper summarizes one numeric vector.

```{r}
#| label: first-function
# Return n, mean, and SD of a numeric vector, rounded.
sbp_summary <- function(x, digits = 1) {
  result <- c(n = length(x), mean = mean(x), sd = sd(x))
  return(round(result, digits))
}

```

## Check the original case, then change the input {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: summary-check-build
identical(sbp_summary(example_sbp), summary_reference)
```

Predict what changes when every measurement increases by 10.

. . .

```{r}
#| label: summary-check-shift
rbind(original = sbp_summary(example_sbp),
      shifted = sbp_summary(example_sbp + 10))
```

The mean increases by 10; the count and SD stay the same.

Matching one example is necessary. Changing the input checks whether the
function actually uses the argument you give it.

## A function wrapper can still use the wrong data {.smaller}

Which calculations below ignore the supplied `x`?

```{r}
#| label: summary-hardcoded
bad_summary <- function(x) {
  return(c(n = length(x), mean = mean(example_sbp), sd = sd(example_sbp)))
}
```

. . .

```{r}
#| label: summary-hardcoded-calls
rbind(first = bad_summary(c(10, 20, 30)),
      second = bad_summary(c(100, 200, 300)))
```

. . .

Only the count uses `x`. The mean and SD still read the external vector.
Repair both references; expect means of `20` and `200` after the repair.


## Call the same function with different inputs {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: first-function-calls
sbp_summary(trial$sbp_0)
sbp_summary(trial$sbp_12)
sbp_summary(trial$weight_kg, digits = 2)
```

. . .

::: {.smaller}
Three calls, one definition. Here we deliberately add a `digits` argument and
round the reported summaries; the earlier duplicated code did not round them.
:::


## Inside an R function object {.smaller #a-function-is-three-things}

```{r}
#| label: anatomy
#| results: hold
formals(sbp_summary)
body(sbp_summary)
environment(sbp_summary)
```

::: {.smaller}
**Formals** — the arguments it accepts, and their defaults ·
**body** — the code it runs · **environment** — where it looks for names it does
not define itself.
:::


## Trace one function call {.smaller}

```r
sbp_summary(c(120, 130, 140), digits = 1)
```

1. Bind `x` to the supplied vector and `digits` to `1` for this call.
2. Evaluate the function body using those local arguments.
3. Create local `result`: `n = 3`, `mean = 130`, and `sd = 10`.
4. `return(round(result, digits))` sends the rounded result to the caller and ends the call.

## Inspect the returned answer {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: trace-call
answer <- sbp_summary(c(120, 130, 140), digits = 1)
answer
answer["mean"]
```

Defining the function stores the recipe. Calling it runs the recipe.

## Missing data requires an explicit design decision {.smaller}

Suppose the new input is `c(120, NA, 140)`. What should `n` mean?

| Policy | Observed count | Reported mean | Reported SD |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Keep missingness in the calculation | 2 | `NA` | `NA` |
| Summarize the observed measurements | 2 | 130 | About 14.1 |

We will define `n` as the **observed count** and add `na_rm = TRUE` as the
default. The caller can choose `FALSE` to preserve missingness in mean and SD.

The count and the missing-data rule are separate decisions. State both.


## Arguments and defaults {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: defaults
# n counts non-missing values, so the reported n matches the mean.
sbp_summary <- function(x, digits = 1, na_rm = TRUE) {
  return(round(c(
    n    = sum(!is.na(x)),
    mean = mean(x, na.rm = na_rm),
    sd   = sd(x, na.rm = na_rm)
  ), digits))
}

```

## Use or override a default {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: defaults-calls
sbp_summary(trial_raw$sbp_12)
sbp_summary(trial_raw$sbp_12, na_rm = FALSE)
```

::: {.smaller}
A default is what the argument is **when the caller says nothing**. Choose the
safe, common case — then let the caller override it.
:::


## How R matches arguments {.smaller}

Three ways, tried in this order: **exact name**, then **partial name**, then
**position**.

```{r}
#| label: matching
sbp_summary(trial$sbp_0, 2)                 # position
sbp_summary(digits = 2, x = trial$sbp_0)    # exact name — order stops mattering
```

. . .

Partial matching works, and is a trap:

```{r}
#| label: matching-error
#| error: true
report <- function(x, na_rm = FALSE, names = TRUE) return("ok")
report(1, n = TRUE)
```

. . .

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**House rule:** data argument by position, everything else by full name. Partial
names break the day somebody adds an argument.
:::


## Make the return explicit {.smaller #return-values-and-the-implicit-return}

Use `return(value)` at every normal exit, including the end of the function.

```{r}
#| label: returns
mean_sbp <- function(x) {
  return(mean(x))
}
quiet_mean <- function(x) {
  return(invisible(mean(x)))
}
mean_sbp(c(120, 140))         # automatically prints 130
quiet_mean(c(120, 140))       # no automatic printing
print(quiet_mean(c(120, 140))) # explicitly prints 130
```

`return()` ends the call. `invisible()` suppresses automatic printing;
the returned value is still available to the caller.


## Choose a return shape for the next step {.smaller}

| Return shape | Useful when | Caller extracts a result with |
|---|---|---|
| One number | The next step needs only one statistic | Use the result directly |
| Named numeric vector | Several results share a numeric type | `answer["mean"]` |
| Named list | Results need different types or structures | `answer$mean` |

Our `sbp_summary()` returns a named numeric vector. A future report might also
need a text status or a table; that would justify a list.

Choose and document the shape before writing downstream code. Changing it
later can break callers even if the numbers are unchanged.

`c(mean = 130, status = "ok")` makes both entries character.
A list can retain the numeric mean and a character status separately.

## Return several results in one list {.smaller #return-several-pieces-in-one-object}

A function returns **one object**. That object can be a list containing several
named results. Here we want the observed count, missing count, and observed mean.

```{r}
#| label: list-result
describe_measurements <- function(x) {
  return(list(n_observed = sum(!is.na(x)),
       n_missing = sum(is.na(x)),
       mean = mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)))
}
```

`return(list(...))` returns the whole list as one object.
It does not return only the last component, `mean`.

## Use the returned components {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: list-components
#| results: hide
description <- describe_measurements(c(120, NA, 140))
description$n_observed
description$n_missing
description$mean
```

| Component | Value | Meaning |
|---|---:|---|
| `n_observed` | 2 | Two measurements are available |
| `n_missing` | 1 | One measurement is missing |
| `mean` | 130 | Mean of 120 and 140; the missing value is excluded |

`description` holds the list; `$` selects a named component. Section 5 adds the
policy for empty or entirely missing input.

## Practice 2: one summary, four named results {.smaller #practice-2-write-a-function}

Write `sbp_summary_missing(x, digits = 1, na_rm = TRUE)` for
`x <- c(120, NA, 140)`. Assume at least two observed numeric values.

| Name | Meaning | Expected value |
|---|---|---:|
| `n` | Observed count | 2 |
| `n_missing` | Missing count | 1 |
| `mean` | Mean of observed values | 130 |
| `sd` | Sample SD of observed values, rounded | 14.1 |

Return **one named numeric vector with these four components**.
Keep the counts unchanged when `na_rm = FALSE`; mean and SD then become `NA`.
Use an explicit `return()` at the end.

## Practice 2: build and return the summary {.smaller #practice-2-answer-and-contract}

```{r}
#| label: summary-missing-extension
sbp_summary_missing <- function(x, digits = 1, na_rm = TRUE) {
  counts <- c(n = sum(!is.na(x)), n_missing = sum(is.na(x)))
  estimates <- c(mean = mean(x, na.rm = na_rm),
                 sd = sd(x, na.rm = na_rm))
  return(c(counts, round(estimates, digits)))
}
answer <- sbp_summary_missing(c(120, NA, 140))
answer
```

The result always has **four named numeric components** in this example.
Counts are separate from the estimates that need rounding.


## Use names to select the intended result {.smaller #extend-the-output-without-changing-its-type}

Reorder the same four components. Which extraction still selects the mean?

```{r}
#| label: summary-named-access
reordered <- answer[c("mean", "sd", "n", "n_missing")]
rbind(
  by_name = c(original = answer[["mean"]],
              reordered = reordered[["mean"]]),
  by_position = c(original = answer[[3]],
                  reordered = reordered[[3]])
)
```

Both vectors have length **4**. `[["mean"]]` gives **130** in either order;
`[[3]]` gives **130** in the original order but **2** after reordering.

Names express what the caller wants; positions depend on the current order.

## What happens inside stays inside {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: locals
centre_sbp <- function(x) {
  offset <- mean(x)      # local to this call
  return(x - offset)
}

centred <- centre_sbp(trial$sbp_0)
round(head(centred, 4), 1)
exists("offset", envir = .GlobalEnv, inherits = FALSE)
```

. . .

::: {.smaller}
Every call gets a **fresh evaluation environment**. Ordinary local assignments
do not change objects in the global workspace.
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
`<<-` writes to the enclosing environment and defeats all of this. You will meet
it in inherited code. Do not write it.
:::


## Forward additional arguments with `...` {.smaller}

`...` collects arguments you did not name and passes them on:

```{r}
#| label: dots
mean_sbp <- function(x, ...) return(mean(x, ...))

mean_sbp(trial_raw$sbp_12)
mean_sbp(trial_raw$sbp_12, na.rm = TRUE)
```

## Return a value without automatically printing it {.smaller}

Use `return(invisible(value))` to return a value without automatic printing.
Explicit output such as `cat()` still appears:

```{r}
#| label: invisible-demo
report_n <- function(data) {
  cat("n =", nrow(data), "\n")
  return(invisible(nrow(data)))
}

report_n(trial)          # prints the message, not the value
n_rows <- report_n(trial)
n_rows
```


# 4 · Scope {.section-divider}


## Where R looks for a name {.smaller}

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| fig-width: 12
flowchart LR
  L["<b>1. Inside the call</b><br/>locals and arguments"] --> D["<b>2. Where the function<br/>was DEFINED</b><br/>usually the global env"]
  D --> P["<b>3. Attached packages</b><br/>dplyr, ggplot2, …"]
  P --> B["<b>4. base</b>"]
  B --> E["Error:<br/>object not found"]
  style L fill:#CFAE70,stroke:#8a7448,color:#fff
  style D fill:#CFAE70,stroke:#8a7448,color:#fff
  style E fill:#f4efe4,stroke:#CFAE70
```

. . .

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
Step 2 is **where the function was written**, not where it was called from. That
is what "lexical" means.
:::


## The global that vanishes {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: scope-works
threshold <- 140

is_high <- function(sbp) return(sbp > threshold)   # threshold is not an argument

sum(is_high(trial$sbp_0))
```

. . .

It works. Now restart R — or hand the script to a colleague:

```{r}
#| label: scope-breaks
#| error: true
rm(threshold)
sum(is_high(trial$sbp_0))
```

. . .

::: {.smaller}
This is the honest failure. It is annoying, and it tells you immediately.
:::


## A hidden input changes the answer {.smaller #the-global-that-is-stale}

This version reads `threshold` from outside the function. It looks up that
variable **each time it is called**; it does not keep its original value.

```{r}
#| label: scope-silent
threshold <- 140
is_high <- function(sbp) return(sbp > threshold)
sum(is_high(trial$sbp_0))
```

. . .

A sensitivity analysis changes the external variable. The same call now uses
that new value:

```{r}
#| label: scope-silent-2
threshold <- 160        # for the sensitivity analysis
sum(is_high(trial$sbp_0))
```

. . .

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
The data and function definition are unchanged. The answer changes because
`threshold` is a hidden input: the first call uses 140 and the second uses 160.
:::


## Everything comes in through an argument {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: scope-fixed
# Flag patients above a systolic threshold. Threshold is an argument so the
# result depends only on what the caller passed.
is_high <- function(sbp, threshold = 140) {
  return(sbp > threshold)
}

sum(is_high(trial$sbp_0))
sum(is_high(trial$sbp_0, threshold = 160))
```

. . .

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**The rule:** a function's return value should depend only on its arguments.
Nothing else.
:::

. . .

::: {.smaller}
The sensitivity analysis is now a second *call*, visible on the page, instead of a
reassignment fifty lines away.
:::


## Practice 3: find the hidden input {.smaller}

```r
reference_mean <- 130
adjust <- function(x) return(x - reference_mean)
first <- adjust(c(120, 140))
reference_mean <- 150
second <- adjust(c(120, 140))
```

1. Predict `first` and `second`.
2. Rewrite `adjust()` so the reference value is a required argument.
3. Explain why restarting R exposes only some global-dependency problems.

## Practice 3: explicit inputs {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: scope-practice-answer
adjust <- function(x, reference_mean) {
  return(x - reference_mean)
}
adjust(c(120, 140), reference_mean = 130)
adjust(c(120, 140), reference_mean = 150)
```

Original results: `c(-10, 10)` and `c(-30, -10)`.

A restart removes a missing global, producing an error. A script that
recreates and later changes that global can still run with the wrong value.

# 5 · Validation {.section-divider}


## Fail loudly, or be wrong quietly {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: silent-wrong
mean_weight <- function(weight_kg) return(mean(weight_kg))

mean_weight(trial_raw$weight_kg)   # one weight is recorded as -99
mean_weight(trial$weight_kg)       # the same cohort, repaired
```

. . .

::: {.smaller}
`r round(mean(trial_raw$weight_kg), 1)` kg against
`r round(mean(trial$weight_kg), 1)` kg. Both are plausible. Only one is right, and
the function had no opinion about which.
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-important}
A function that fails loudly on bad input is safer than one that returns a
plausible wrong answer.
:::


## `stopifnot()` {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: stopifnot-demo
#| error: true
checked_mean <- function(x, digits = 1) {
  stopifnot(is.numeric(x), length(x) > 0, digits >= 0)

  return(round(mean(x, na.rm = TRUE), digits))
}

checked_mean(trial$arm)
```

## Give failed checks a useful message {.smaller}

Name the checks and you choose the message:

```{r}
#| label: stopifnot-named
#| error: true
checked_mean <- function(x, digits = 1) {
  stopifnot(
    "x must be a numeric vector" = is.numeric(x),
    "digits must not be negative" = digits >= 0
  )
  return(round(mean(x, na.rm = TRUE), digits))
}

checked_mean(trial$arm)
```


## `stop()` and guard clauses {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: guard-clause
#| error: true
# Mean weight, refusing sentinel codes. Site 3 used -99 for "not recorded",
# and averaging those understates the mean by about 3 kg.
mean_weight <- function(weight_kg) {
  if (any(weight_kg < 20, na.rm = TRUE)) {
    stop("weight_kg contains values below 20: check for sentinel codes",
         call. = FALSE)
  }
  return(mean(weight_kg, na.rm = TRUE))
}

mean_weight(trial_raw$weight_kg)
```

. . .

::: {.smaller}
A **guard clause** is a check at the top that exits early. It keeps the happy path
unindented and the failure cases visible.
:::


## How much validation is enough {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size:0.9em"}
| Check | Because |
|---|---|
| **Type and shape** | `is.numeric()`, `is.data.frame()`, `length()`, column names present |
| **Values that cannot be real** | Negative weights, ages over 120, proportions above 1 |
| **What your code silently assumes** | Sorted rows, one row per patient, non-empty groups |
:::

. . .

::: {.smaller}
`mean("a")` warns and returns `NA`; it does not stop. Validate numeric input
when a missing result would hide a data-type error.
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
Rule of thumb: validate what a **collaborator's file** could plausibly get wrong.
Two or three checks is usually right.
:::


## Specify the edge cases {.smaller}

Our `safe_mean()` contract accepts numeric vectors with finite values or `NA`/`NaN`.
It returns **one numeric value** and ignores missing observations.

| Input | Required behavior |
|---|---|
| `c(2, 4, NA)` | Return `3` |
| `numeric(0)` | Return `NA_real_` |
| `c(NA_real_, NA_real_)` | Return `NA_real_` |
| `"4"`, a matrix, or a data frame | Stop with a useful message |
| `c(2, Inf)` | Stop because infinity is outside this contract |

`NA_real_` explicitly creates numeric missingness. `c(NA, NA)` is logical,
so use typed missing values when constructing a numeric teaching column.

## Build `safe_mean()` with guard clauses {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: safe-mean
safe_mean <- function(x) {
  if (!is.numeric(x) || !is.null(dim(x))) {
    stop("x must be a numeric vector", call. = FALSE)
  }
  if (any(is.infinite(x))) {
    stop("x must not contain infinite values", call. = FALSE)
  }
  if (all(is.na(x))) return(NA_real_)
  return(mean(x, na.rm = TRUE))
}
safe_mean(c(2, 4, NA))
safe_mean(numeric(0))
```

The empty case also exits because `all(logical(0))` is `TRUE`.

## Trace the branch that ends the call {.smaller}

Follow `safe_mean()` from top to bottom. Stop tracing when a guard exits.

| Input | First exit | Result | Does `mean()` run? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `"4"` | Type guard: `stop()` | Error | No |
| `c(2, Inf)` | Infinite-value guard: `stop()` | Error | No |
| `c(NA_real_, NA_real_)` | `return(NA_real_)` | One numeric `NA` | No |
| `c(2, NA, 4)` | Last expression | `3` | Yes |

For `numeric(0)`, the first two guards pass and `all(is.na(x))` is `TRUE`.
The early return supplies one numeric `NA`, not an empty vector.

## Explain why the shorter version changes the contract {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: mean-shortcut
mean_shortcut <- function(x) return(mean(x, na.rm = TRUE))
mean_shortcut(numeric(0))
safe_mean(numeric(0))
```

Both run. The first returns `NaN`; our helper returns `NA_real_` by design.

Ask which behavior a report expects, and document it. A shorter implementation
is useful only if it preserves the intended input and output rules.

## Practice 4: choose the checks {.smaller}

Complete the contract for `centre_values(x, centre)`.

```r
centre_values <- function(x, centre = 0) {
  stopifnot(
    "x must be a numeric vector" = is.numeric(x) && is.null(dim(x)),
    "centre must be one finite number" = # your condition
  )
  return(x - centre)
}
```

Reject `centre = c(1, 2)`, `NA`, `Inf`, and `"2"`. In what order should
the checks run so each later check can safely assume the earlier ones passed?

## Practice 4: answer and checks {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: validate-centre
centre_values <- function(x, centre = 0) {
  stopifnot(
    "x must be a numeric vector" = is.numeric(x) && is.null(dim(x)),
    "centre must be one finite number" =
      is.numeric(centre) && length(centre) == 1 &&
      is.null(dim(centre)) && is.finite(centre)
  )
  return(x - centre)
}
stopifnot(identical(centre_values(c(1, NA, 3), centre = 2),
                    c(-1, NA, 1)))
```

Validate the type, then the length, then the value. An expected failure is
also evidence that the interface works; try `centre_values(1:3, centre = NA)`.

# 6 · Data-frame functions {.section-divider}


## Data argument first {.smaller}

When the column names are fixed, nothing special is needed:

```{r}
#| label: df-function
# Add change from baseline; check the required columns before computing.
add_change <- function(data) {
  stopifnot(is.data.frame(data),
            all(c("sbp_0", "sbp_12") %in% names(data)))

  return(data |> mutate(change = sbp_12 - sbp_0))
}

trial_raw |> add_change() |> summarise(mean_change = mean(change, na.rm = TRUE))
```

. . .

::: {.smaller}
**Data first**, so the function drops into a pipeline like any dplyr verb.
:::


## Pass a bare column name with double braces {.smaller}

When the **column itself** is the argument, dplyr needs to be told:

```{r}
#| label: tidyeval
summarise_by_arm <- function(data, outcome) {
  result <- data |>
    group_by(arm) |>
    summarise(
      n    = sum(!is.na({{ outcome }})),
      mean = round(mean({{ outcome }}, na.rm = TRUE), 1)
    )
  return(result)
}

```

## Call the column-aware helper {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: tidyeval-calls
summarise_by_arm(trial_raw, sbp_12)
summarise_by_arm(trial_raw, weight_kg)
```

::: {.smaller}
```r
# the base R way — no tidy evaluation involved
tapply(trial_raw$sbp_12, trial_raw$arm, mean, na.rm = TRUE)
```
:::


## Without double braces: two failures {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: tidyeval-fail
#| error: true
bad_summary <- function(data, outcome) {
  return(data |> group_by(arm) |> summarise(mean = mean(outcome)))
}

bad_summary(trial, sbp_0)
```

## A stray global can produce a plausible wrong answer {.smaller}

Now the same call, with a stray object in the workspace:

```{r}
#| label: tidyeval-silent
sbp_0 <- c(1000, 2000)      # left over from something else entirely
bad_summary(trial, sbp_0)
```

```{r}
#| label: tidyeval-cleanup
#| include: false
rm(sbp_0)
```


## A quoted column name with base R {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: string-column
summarise_column <- function(data, column) {
  stopifnot(is.data.frame(data), is.character(column),
            length(column) == 1, !is.na(column),
            column %in% names(data))
  return(safe_mean(data[[column]]))
}
summarise_column(trial_raw, "sbp_12")
```

`data[[column]]` looks up the value of `column`. `data$column` looks for a
column literally named `column`.

Use <code>&#123;&#123; outcome &#125;&#125;</code> for a bare-name dplyr interface and `[[column]]` for a
quoted-name base R interface. State which interface the function expects.

# 7 · Refactoring and reuse {.section-divider #refactoring}


## Before: the script we all wrote {.smaller}

```r
# baseline
tab_0 <- trial_raw |> group_by(arm) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean = round(mean(sbp_0), 1), sd = round(sd(sbp_0), 1))

# 12 weeks
tab_12 <- trial_raw |> group_by(arm) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean = round(mean(sbp_12), 1), sd = round(sd(sbp_12), 1))

# change — use the extract with missing outcomes
tab_ch <- trial_raw |> group_by(arm) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean = round(mean(change, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
            sd = round(sd(change), 1))     # <- na.rm missing here

ggplot(trial_raw, aes(arm, sbp_0)) + geom_boxplot() + labs(y = "SBP baseline")
ggplot(trial_raw, aes(arm, sbp_12)) + geom_boxplot() + labs(y = "SBP 12 wk")
ggplot(trial_raw, aes(arm, change)) + geom_boxplot() + labs(y = "Change")
```

. . .

::: {.smaller}
Six blocks, two shapes, **inconsistent missing-value rules**.
`n = n()` counts rows, including rows missing the outcome.
:::


## After: the summary helper {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: refactor
#| results: hold
# n counts patients contributing to the mean, not patients randomised.
summarise_by_arm <- function(data, outcome, digits = 1) {
  stopifnot(is.data.frame(data), "arm" %in% names(data))

  result <- data |>
    group_by(arm) |>
    summarise(
      n    = sum(!is.na({{ outcome }})),
      mean = round(mean({{ outcome }}, na.rm = TRUE), digits),
      sd   = round(sd({{ outcome }}, na.rm = TRUE), digits)
    )
  return(result)
}

```

## After: the plotting helper {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: refactor-plot-helper
# One boxplot of an outcome by arm, labelled for a clinical reader.
plot_by_arm <- function(data, outcome, y_label) {
  plot <- ggplot(data, aes(arm, {{ outcome }}, fill = arm)) +
    geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, width = 0.5) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = y_label) +
    theme(legend.position = "none")
  return(plot)
}

summarise_by_arm(trial_raw, change)
```


## Verify the refactor {.smaller}

A refactor preserves intended behavior. Fix a known bug separately, then
compare the function with that corrected reference. **Check.**

```{r}
#| label: verify
old <- trial |>
  group_by(arm) |>
  summarise(n = sum(!is.na(sbp_0)),
            mean = round(mean(sbp_0), 1),
            sd = round(sd(sbp_0), 1))

new <- summarise_by_arm(trial, sbp_0)

identical(old, new)
all.equal(old, new)
```

## Interpret the comparison {.smaller}

::: {.smaller}
`identical()` checks exact equality. `all.equal()` returns `TRUE` or a description
of differences. Use `isTRUE(all.equal(old, new))` for a logical check.
:::


## Compose two functions for paired measurements {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: classify-change
classify_change <- function(change) {
  stopifnot(is.numeric(change), is.null(dim(change)))
  out <- rep("missing", length(change))
  observed <- !is.na(change)
  out[observed & change < 0] <- "decrease"
  out[observed & change >= 0] <- "no decrease"
  return(out)
}
classify_change(c(-2, 1, NA, 0))
```

This returns a character vector even for zero rows. It describes the sign
of change, not whether a change is clinically meaningful.

## A reusable paired-change calculation {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: change-summary
change_summary <- function(baseline, followup) {
  stopifnot(is.numeric(baseline), is.null(dim(baseline)),
            is.numeric(followup), is.null(dim(followup)),
            length(baseline) == length(followup),
            !any(is.infinite(baseline)), !any(is.infinite(followup)))
  change <- followup - baseline
  return(data.frame(change = change, category = classify_change(change)))
}
change_summary(c(10, 8, NA, 12), c(8, 9, 7, 12))
```

**Precondition:** the two vectors refer to the same people in the same order.
Equal lengths do not establish patient alignment; join by ID first when needed.

## Practice 5: verify the refactor {.smaller}

Before replacing the repeated code, write down the expected table.

```r
baseline <- c(10, 8, NA, 12)
followup <- c(8, 9, 7, 12)
expected <- data.frame(
  change = c(-2, 1, NA, 0),
  category = c("decrease", "no decrease", "missing", "no decrease")
)
```

1. Compare `change_summary(baseline, followup)` with `expected`.
2. Try two empty numeric vectors. What are the output column types?
3. Try unequal lengths. Why should recycling be an error here?

## Practice 5: evidence before replacement {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: refactor-evidence
expected <- data.frame(
  change = c(-2, 1, NA, 0),
  category = c("decrease", "no decrease", "missing", "no decrease")
)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(
  change_summary(c(10, 8, NA, 12), c(8, 9, 7, 12)), expected
)))
str(change_summary(numeric(0), numeric(0)))
```

Keep the corrected reference until the comparison passes. A bug correction
may change results; record that change separately from reorganizing the code.

## Save a helper separately from the analysis {.smaller}

Keep reusable definitions in an `.R` file and analysis calls in your report:

```text
work/session11/
  functions-lab.qmd       # or functions-lab.Rmd
  R/
    centre-values.R
    functions.R          # your other completed helpers
```

The supplied `R/centre-values.R` contains the validated `centre_values()`.
It defines the function; it does not load data or run an analysis.

**Editing the file does not update a function already in memory.**
Save it, then source it again or render the report again.

## Load the saved definition, then call it {.smaller}

In the saved report, with paths relative to its folder:

```r
source("R/centre-values.R")
centre_values(c(10, NA, 14), centre = 12)
# [1] -2 NA  2
```

In the Console, use the path from your personal project root:

```r
source(here::here("work", "session11", "R", "centre-values.R"))
```

`source()` executes the file's R expressions. The function definition binds its
name; the later call supplies data and returns centered values.


## Reuse should survive a fresh session {.smaller}

1. Copy the supplied `R` folder beside your report.
2. Put your other completed helpers in `R/functions.R`.
3. Add both `source()` calls to the report before the first function call.
4. Remove duplicate definitions from the report after checking equivalence.
5. Restart R and render the report using its saved source.

If a function is missing, inspect the source path and execution order.
If an old result persists, check which file or later definition replaced it.

**Evidence:** the fresh render reproduces the expected values and checks
without manually running definitions in the Console first.

## House style for functions {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size:0.88em"}
| Rule | In practice |
|---|---|
| **Verbs for functions, nouns for objects** | `summarise_by_arm()`, not `arm_summary()` |
| **`snake_case`, no exceptions** | `plot_by_arm`, not `plotByArm` |
| **One job per function** | If the name needs "and", it is two functions |
| **Make exits explicit** | Use `return(value)` at every normal exit |
| **Keep it focused** | A long function is a reason to review its responsibilities |
| **Data argument first** | So it pipes |
| **Validate inputs** | Two or three checks, at the top |
| **One line above saying what it does** | What it takes, what it returns |
| **Comments say *why*** | The code already says what |
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
All of this is in `style-guide.md`, §7. **Code quality is graded on it.**
:::

1. Why does `if (c(TRUE, FALSE)) ...` fail? What tool produces one label per row?
2. What should `safe_mean(c(NA_real_, NA_real_))` return under today's contract?
3. Why can a function's answer change when its definition has not changed?
4. How does a quoted column name differ from a bare column argument?
5. What evidence should you collect before deleting the original repeated code?

## Summary {.smaller}

- `if` controls one decision; vectorized conditionals classify many values.
- A function is an interface: arguments in, one predictable result out.
- Local objects and explicit arguments avoid stale global dependencies.
- Guard clauses turn silent wrong answers into informative failures.
- Refactoring is complete only after the new result matches a trusted result.
